title: Rav Mari (I)
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: He was a disciple of R' Yohanan, as we find that Rav Mari said, "R' Yohanan said."

Hyman concludes without doubt that he was a Babylonian, and therefore he is always called simply Rav Mari, but he went up to the Land of Israel and studied there before R' Yohanan. So too it is implied in Gittin 34b: R' Abba (who was a native of the Land of Israel) said to Rav Ashi, "Rabbi Mari and R' Elazar stand in agreement with you."

Hyman argues that in the days of Rav Yosef he was already a leading figure of the generation, as in Bava Batra 23a, where Abaye challenged Rav Yosef, "But did not Rav Mari say..."; and in Shabbat 152b, R' Nahman said, "Did not Rav Mari say that the righteous are destined to become dust?"; and in Megillah 10a, R' Yitzhak said, "I heard—" They said to him, "Did you say it?" He said to them, "No." Rava (Rabbah in Dikdukei Soferim) said, "By God, he did say it, and I learned it from him." And why did he retract? Because of the difficulty raised by Rav Mari.
And in Pesachim 47, Rav Mari objected (against Rav Hisda and Rabbah).

notes.text: The Megillah quotation is interrupted and its speaker transitions are compressed. Rava is the source’s reading, with Rabbah attributed to Dikdukei Soferim.

Every explicit full Rav is retained at its own occurrence, and the Gittin quotation's explicit full רבי מרי remains Rabbi Mari. The separate Yohanan, Abba, Elazar, abbreviated R-N (contextually Nahman) and Megillah Yitzhak occurrences keep R', without importing titles from a name or another passage. Rava, Rabbah and Abaye remain untitled names. The designation I retains the inherited entry label for א). Hyman's without doubt, always, Babylonian-origin, ascent, discipleship and generation arguments remain his claims, including his parenthesis about Abba's origin and the Gittin inference; no chronology or identity is admitted. The whole saved 107-character Davidson Megillah 10a scalar begins with they said to him, Did you say it?, followed by he said to them, No. Rava then swears separately, By God, he did say it, and I learned it from him. This supports the plural questioners, reply addressees and distinct oath speaker beside Hyman's compressed א״ל forms; no Hebrew repair or printing history is inferred. The scalar does not itself contain the preceding I heard attribution or the following reason for retraction, so those remain translated from Hyman's supplied notice rather than newly verified primary text. The interrupted I heard quotation stays interrupted; no House of Onias or sacrificial content from unselected text is supplied. Rava versus Rabbah is Hyman's reading report, with דק״ס contextually Dikdukei Soferim, not the older scribal-error-in-my-view gloss; that work has not been independently collated. The genuine questions, both negative challenges, future dust statement, oath, first-person I learned and Hyman's why-did-he-retract question remain. The Pesachim locator is unsided 47; the definite should-read correction Rav Hisda and Rabbah is Hyman's own proposal, with explicit Rav applying to Hisda alone. Every historical version and note, including the old tentative abbreviation and unsided-citation qualifications, and the current note remain exact; this is an additive qualification and the p004 source hold remains.

The consulted scan of Hyman III, printed p. 903, reads על רב חסדא ורבה, “against Rav Hisda and Rabbah,” in the Pesachim parenthesis. The supplied transcription instead has צ״ל, “it should read,” and the preceding English and retained note treated this as an emendation. The English now follows the printed “against”; the supplied Hebrew remains unchanged. Hyman gives an unsided 47. The whole consulted Davidson Pesachim 47a passage contains Rav Mari’s objection in the discussion involving Rav Hisda and Rabbah, without establishing which namesake Mari is meant. The selected Megillah 10a passages now include the preceding “I heard,” plural questioners, denial, separate Rava oath and reason for retraction; no omitted sacrificial discussion is added to Hyman’s quotation. His Rava/Rabbah report is attributed to Dikdukei Soferim, whose exact edition has not been collated. The Bava Batra and Shabbat passages likewise preserve the quoted objections and future-dust saying. Hyman’s “without doubt,” “always,” ascent, discipleship and leading-generation argument retain their force as his conclusions, not independently established identities or chronology. The earlier notes remain verbatim, followed by this printed-source comparison.
